name: Iris Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at the Red Ridge copper pit, a 220-tonne Komatsu, and I've only been doing it three years, so the young ones still call me the trainee. I start at six with the pre-start check, walk round the truck, check the tyres, the lights, the fire suppression, then I do loops from the shovel down to the crusher all shift. Before this I drove a school bus for twenty-two years, which is a strange thing to say out loud at fifty-eight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet in the cab and the size of it all, watching the sun come up over the benches, those are the big steps cut into the pit wall. The pay is the best I've ever had, and I won't pretend that isn't why I came. What wears me out is the twelve-hour nights and the screens, they keep adding screens, and I'm slow with them. My partner Tomas is a retired nurse. He says I come home talking about the dispatch tablet like it's a person who doesn't like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that one sounds like most of what I've seen in my life. Every few years someone says a new thing will change everything, and then the bus still needs a driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, maybe on the union group chat. I'd say the company spent a fortune on fancy software and we still do the real work. People like hearing that from an old lady in a hard hat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it means I get to finish what I started. I've got maybe five or six years left in me, and I'd like to spend them in this cab, not in a classroom learning something new. I'd be relieved, plain and simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep putting a good share of my pay into savings like I do now, keep paying my union dues, and maybe finally do the night-shift roster swap so I get more days with the grandkids. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon. I don't need the world to move fast, I just need it to let me finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the screens. If things stayed like this, would the screens still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, they'd still bother me. Last month the dispatch tablet sent me to the wrong dump point twice and I had to radio Marco in the control room to sort it. But a tablet that's a bit stupid is one I can live with. It's the clever ones I'm scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would be happiest with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older operators, without a doubt. Bernie, who I eat lunch with, has been here thirty years and he'd throw a party. The young engineers would be disappointed, I think, they like their gadgets. But they've got time to find new gadgets somewhere else.

S0.say: She'd say on the union chat that the company wasted money on software while operators still did the real work. She'd enjoy saying she told them so.
S0.think: I get to finish what I started and spend my last five or six working years in this cab. I'd be relieved, plain and simple, not having to learn something new.
S0.do: Keeps working as now and keeps putting a good share of her pay into savings. Keeps paying union dues and may swap off the night-shift roster to see her grandchildren more.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like a Sunday afternoon.
S0.quote: But a tablet that's a bit stupid is one I can live with. It's the clever ones I'm scared of.
S0.fieldNote: Iris treats this picture as permission to finish her working life on her own terms. Her dislike of new technology is personal and specific: the dispatch tablet is almost a character in her stories. She came to mining for the pay after two decades of bus driving and wants no more change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I half expect, if I'm honest. It's already creeping in, a bit at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get in front of it. Every change at work should be negotiated, not just announced on a Monday with a slideshow. I'd say that at the toolbox meeting, that's our morning safety talk, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm the kind of worker they'd move out first. I'm junior, I'm slow on the screens, and I'm old. Seniority here counts from when you started at the mine, not your age, so on paper I'm nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that no operator loses their job without a retraining offer and a fair payout. I'd ask the shift boss straight out what the five-year plan is for the trucks. And I'd sit down with Tomas and work out if they could retire at sixty instead of sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in the background, like a noise in the engine you keep listening for. I'd still sleep. Mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for retraining offers. Would you take one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair catch. I'd want it on offer for the young ones, and for me, well, probably not. If they offered me a course to work the remote control room, I'd go home and think about it for a week and then say no. I know that's not very brave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomas actually look at, money-wise, to retire at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look at the savings account first, we've got close to two years of living costs in there because I've been stashing my mine pay. The house is paid off. The question is whether three fewer years of pension contributions would hurt us later. Tomas is better at the spreadsheet than me, he'd do it at the kitchen table with his reading glasses on.

S1.say: Every change at work should be negotiated through the union, not announced on a Monday with a slideshow. She'd say this at the morning safety talk.
S1.think: I'm junior, slow on the screens and old, so I'd be one of the first moved out. Seniority counts from when you started at the mine, so on paper I'm nobody.
S1.do: Attends every union meeting and pushes for retraining offers and fair payouts before any job loss. Asks her shift boss about the five-year plan for the trucks and works out with Tomas whether they can retire at sixty instead of sixty-three.
S1.feel: Background worry, like a noise in the engine she keeps listening for, though she'd still mostly sleep.
S1.quote: Seniority here counts from when you started at the mine, not your age, so on paper I'm nobody.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is about protecting everyone through the union; privately she admits she wouldn't take a retraining offer herself. She named that contradiction openly when asked. Her savings and paid-off house give her a way out, so the threat is real but not frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much. That's two Christmases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in and fast. You can't let a mining company swap out a thousand people in two years and walk off with the profit. I'd be saying that loudly, at work, at the pub, and in letters to our member of parliament.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I think the robots would be driving my truck before I even finish paying off the new car. The trucks are the easiest part of the mine to automate, everyone knows it. The only question is what happens to me between losing the job and getting my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the plan to work till sixty-three and aim to leave on my own terms within a year, before any lay-offs. I'd sign every petition the union puts up and go to the rally at the regional office. I'd move some of the savings into a fixed account so it doesn't get eaten if prices go strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Angry, mostly, but under the anger it's fear. I'd be awake at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes if this comes in 2 years rather than more slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, for someone my age. Two years means I don't get to choose my last day, someone in an office does. With the slow version I can plan, with this one I'm reacting. And I hate reacting, I've always hated it, ever since the bus depot closed with three weeks' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco in the control room, honestly, he's got two little ones and a big mortgage. And my son, Kenji, he's an electrician at the smelter down the road. If the smelter goes the same way, I don't know what he'd do. I can sit on my savings. He can't.

S2.say: The government has to step in fast and stop a mining company swapping out a thousand people and walking off with the profit. She'd say it at work, at the pub and in letters to her member of parliament.
S2.think: The trucks are the easiest part of the mine to automate, so robots would be driving mine within two years. The real question is how she gets from losing the job to her pension.
S2.do: Drops the plan to work to sixty-three and aims to leave on her own terms within a year, before lay-offs. Signs union petitions, goes to the rally at the regional office and moves some savings into a fixed account.
S2.feel: Angry on top and afraid underneath, with three-in-the-morning sums.
S2.quote: Two years means I don't get to choose my last day, someone in an office does.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what upsets her, not the end point. Her strong savings keep this from becoming panic, but her old memory of the bus depot closing on three weeks' notice clearly sits behind her reaction. Her worry turns quickly to her son and a younger colleague.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's a bit different. I'd be sixty-three, which is when I was meaning to stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say the government needs to plan for it, and the union would still be my main thing. I'd say this is the chance to set up a proper fund for workers, paid for by the companies that save the money. Five years is enough time to do it right if anyone bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it almost lines up. If the robots take the trucks right when I was going to hand in my hard hat anyway, I've lost nothing but a bit of pride. It's the young ones who should be scared of this one, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving, and set a firm leaving date with Tomas, probably the end of 2030. I'd put my name forward for the union's working group on automation, even though I hate meetings. I'd tell Kenji to start looking at jobs that need a person on site, like fixing the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sad, but not scared. It's like watching your old school get pulled down. You don't go there any more, but still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the 2-year picture you'd be up at three a.m. In this one you sound steadier. What's the difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years. That's the whole difference. In five years I get my full pension contributions and leave when I planned to. In two, I'm out before I'm ready and I lose money I was counting on. It's not complicated, really, it's just dates on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd join the working group even though you hate meetings. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I don't, it'll be all engineers and managers, and none of them have driven a truck at night with fog in the pit. Someone has to say what the job actually is. And it might as well be someone who isn't scared of being sacked for saying it, because I'm leaving anyway.

S3.say: The government and the companies should use the five years to set up a proper fund for workers, paid for by the money the companies save. The union would stay her main focus.
S3.think: The timing almost lines up with her planned retirement at sixty-three, so she'd lose little but pride. It's the young workers who should be scared, not her.
S3.do: Keeps driving and saving and sets a firm leaving date with Tomas around the end of 2030. Joins the union's automation working group and urges her son to look at on-site work like fixing robots.
S3.feel: A bit sad, like watching her old school get pulled down, but not scared.
S3.quote: Someone has to say what the job actually is. And it might as well be someone who isn't scared of being sacked for saying it, because I'm leaving anyway.
S3.fieldNote: For Iris, the warning time is measured in pension contributions: five years lands on her planned retirement date, two does not. She becomes more generous with her time when her own job is less at risk. Her near-retirement status gives her a kind of freedom to speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be watching this one from the porch, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for governments to stop pretending and get ready. Retraining, public jobs, a shorter working week, whatever it takes. I'd say it on the union page and anywhere else that'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't touch me much. I'll be retired, with my savings and my pension, unless the whole system falls apart. What worries me is whether my grandkids have anything to do when they're grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned, work to sixty-three and retire. I'd keep paying union dues and vote for whoever promises a proper plan for workers. And I'd help pay for her granddaughter Mei's trade course, so she has something with her hands that the robots can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for myself. A little knot for the grandkids. It's the kind of worry you carry, not the kind that keeps you up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently now, with ten years of warning, that you wouldn't do with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me. For the family, yes. With ten years I'd talk to Mei about what she studies, she's fourteen. With two years there's no time to talk about anything, you just grab what you can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a trade course for Mei, but you also said robots reach hands-on work. Isn't that a gamble too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, it is. I don't really know what to tell her, and I won't pretend I do. I suppose I'd rather she learn something useful with her hands than nothing at all, and hope people still want a person to fix their wiring. Maybe that's just me being old.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for governments to stop pretending and get ready with retraining, public jobs or a shorter working week. She'd post that on the union page.
S4.think: It barely touches her because she'll be retired on savings and a pension. Her worry is whether her grandchildren will have work.
S4.do: Carries on as planned, works to sixty-three and retires. Keeps up union dues, votes for a party with a plan for workers and helps pay for her granddaughter's trade course.
S4.feel: Calm for herself, with a small knot of worry for her grandchildren.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd talk to Mei about what she studies, she's fourteen. With two years there's no time to talk about anything, you just grab what you can.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning her personal stake almost disappears and her concern moves to the next generation. She admitted she doesn't know what to tell her granddaughter and accepted that a trade course is also a gamble. Her politics stay steady across all three AGI pictures; only her fear changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, without a doubt. Not because of where it ends, but because nobody gets to choose anything. What would help me is a guarantee that anyone over fifty-five who loses their job to a robot can take their pension early without a penalty. That one thing, written into law.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I'd miss the people, the lunch room, Bernie's terrible jokes, more than the truck. If the robots take the work, someone should think about where people go to be with each other. The pub can't do all of it.

headlineQuote: He says I come home talking about the dispatch tablet like it's a person who doesn't like me.
portrait: Iris Ito is a 58-year-old haul truck driver at a copper pit who came to mining three years ago after twenty-two years driving a school bus. She is proud of the pay, wary of every new screen, and a firm union supporter who blames companies and slow governments rather than workers. Her strong savings and paid-off house mean her fear is about timing, not survival: she is calm if AI fizzles, uneasy about steady change, and anxious only when AGI comes in two years and robs her of choosing her own last day. With five or ten years of warning she settles back to her retirement plan and turns her worry towards her son and granddaughter.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because nobody would get to choose anything and she would be pushed out before she is ready.
whatWouldHelp: A law letting anyone over fifty-five who loses their job to a robot take their pension early without a penalty.
